hints: Recall what you know about the ends of the period: sodium oxide forms an alkaline solution while sulfur oxides form acidic solutions, with aluminium oxide in the middle being amphoteric.
walkthrough:
Picture the two ends of the period**
Think of sodium on the left. Its oxide, $\text{Na}_2\text{O}$, dissolves to give $\text{OH}^-$ ions, so it is strongly basic. Now jump to sulfur on the right. Its oxides, $\text{SO}_2$ and $\text{SO}_3$, dissolve to give $\text{H}^+$ ions, so they are strongly acidic. In the middle, $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ can act as both.
Final answer: The oxides become more acidic / less basic from Na to S.

hints: Write out the formulae of the highest oxides: $\text{Na}_2\text{O}$, $\text{MgO}$, $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$, $\text{SiO}_2$, $\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$, $\text{SO}_3$, and work out the oxidation number of the Period 3 element in each.
Link that oxidation number to the electronic configuration of the element, focusing on how many electrons are in the outer shell that can be lost or shared with oxygen.
walkthrough:
Work out the pattern in numbers**
Oxygen is almost always $-2$. So in $\text{Na}_2\text{O}$ Na is $+1$, in $\text{MgO}$ Mg is $+2$, in $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ Al is $+3$, in $\text{SiO}_2$ Si is $+4$, in $\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$ P is $+5$, in $\text{SO}_3$ S is $+6$. The maximum oxidation number clearly rises by one each step.

Explain it with electrons**
Sodium is $[\text{Ne}]3s^1$ with one outer electron to lose or share, magnesium has two, aluminium three, and so on up to sulfur with six. The maximum number of electrons the atom can use in bonding to oxygen increases across the period, so the maximum oxidation number increases.

Final answer: Maximum oxidation number increases from +1 (Na) to +6 (S).
This is because the number of valence / outer shell electrons increases from 1 to 6 across the period.

hints: Remember the general rule: a basic metal oxide plus water gives an alkali, while an acidic non-metal oxide plus water gives an acid.
Think of the familiar alkali made from sodium and the familiar phosphorus containing acid where P keeps its +5 oxidation state.
walkthrough:
Sort basic from acidic**
$\text{Na}_2\text{O}$ is a strongly basic oxide. Adding water simply adds $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ to the oxide ion to make hydroxide ions: $$\text{Na}_2\text{O} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 2\text{NaOH}$$ So the named product is sodium hydroxide.

Name the acid from phosphorus(V) oxide**
$\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$ is a strongly acidic oxide. With water it forms the phosphorus(V) containing acid where P is still +5: $$\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10} + 6\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 4\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$$ So the named product is phosphoric(V) acid.

Final answer: sodium oxide with water: sodium hydroxide
phosphorus(V) oxide with water: phosphoric(V) acid

hints: Compare the structures: phosphorus(V) oxide exists as discrete $\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$ molecules while magnesium oxide forms a continuous lattice of ions.
Ask yourself what must be broken to melt each solid: separating whole molecules apart, or pulling apart oppositely charged ions.
Relate the amount of energy needed to melt to the relative strength of those two different types of attraction.
walkthrough:
See what phosphorus(V) oxide really is**
Do not picture a giant network. $\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$ exists as separate, discrete molecules. The covalent P-O bonds inside each molecule are strong and stay intact when it melts. All you break on melting is the weak attractions between one molecule and its neighbour, the intermolecular / van der Waals forces. Little energy is needed, so melting is easy.

See what magnesium oxide really is**
Now picture the opposite. $\text{MgO}$ is a giant ionic lattice with $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ and $\text{O}^{2-}$ ions packed together in all directions. There are no molecules. To melt it you must pull apart huge numbers of oppositely charged ions, breaking strong electrostatic attractions / ionic bonds throughout the lattice.

Compare strengths to explain the numbers**
Weak intermolecular forces need only a small amount of thermal energy to overcome, hence about $300^{\circ}\text{C}$ is enough for $\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$. Strong ionic attractions need a very large amount of thermal energy, hence about $2850^{\circ}\text{C}$ is needed for $\text{MgO}$. The difference in melting point is a direct measure of the difference in strength of the forces broken.

Final answer: Phosphorus(V) oxide is simple molecular, only weak intermolecular forces / van der Waals forces between $\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$ molecules are broken on melting.
Magnesium oxide is giant ionic, strong electrostatic forces of attraction between $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ and $\text{O}^{2-}$ ions must be broken on melting.
Intermolecular forces are much weaker than ionic bonds, so much less energy is needed to melt phosphorus(V) oxide, giving a much lower melting point.

hints: Treat this as a normal base plus acid reaction: the oxide ion will become water and aluminium will form the salt aluminium chloride, then balance Al, Cl, H and O.
walkthrough:
Build the equation as base plus acid**
Here $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ acts as a base. The $\text{O}^{2-}$ combines with $\text{H}^+$ from $\text{HCl}$ to make $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, and $\text{Al}^{3+}$ joins with $\text{Cl}^-$ to make $\text{AlCl}_3$. Balancing gives: $$\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 + 6\text{HCl} \rightarrow 2\text{AlCl}_3 + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ Check atoms: 2 Al, 3 O, 6 H, 6 Cl on both sides.
Final answer: $\mathrm{Al_2O_3 + 6HCl \rightarrow 2AlCl_3 + 3H_2O}$

hints: Remember that with excess concentrated alkali aluminium forms the soluble complex ion $\text{Al(OH)}_4^-$, so combine $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ with $\text{NaOH}$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ to make $\text{NaAl(OH)}_4$.
walkthrough:
Build the equation as acid plus alkali**
Here $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ acts as an acid. With excess aqueous $\text{NaOH}$ it forms sodium aluminate, best written as $\text{NaAl(OH)}_4$ containing the $\text{Al(OH)}_4^-$ ion. Water is needed to supply extra $\text{OH}$ groups: $$\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 + 2\text{NaOH} + 3\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 2\text{NaAl(OH)}_4$$ This shows amphoteric behaviour clearly.
Final answer: $\mathrm{Al_2O_3 + 2NaOH + 3H_2O \rightarrow 2NaAl(OH)_4}$

hints: Recall that silicon(IV) oxide has a very high melting point similar to diamond, which tells you whether it is simple molecular or giant.
Think about how many bonds silicon forms and how oxygen bridges between silicons, focusing on the shape around each Si atom.
walkthrough:
Recognise the giant network**
$\text{SiO}_2$ is not made of separate molecules. It is a giant covalent / macromolecular solid, a continuous 3D network of strong Si-O covalent bonds extending in all directions. That is why it is hard and has a very high melting point.

Describe the arrangement**
Picture each silicon atom at the centre of a tetrahedron, joined by single covalent bonds to four oxygen atoms. Each oxygen atom in turn bridges two silicon atoms ($\text{Si-O-Si}$). This tetrahedral arrangement repeats throughout the lattice.

Final answer: Giant covalent lattice.
Each Si is tetrahedrally bonded to four O atoms / each Si forms four Si-O bonds, each O bridges two Si atoms.

hints: This is a simple combination of a basic oxide and an acidic oxide with no other products, so just add the two reactants together to give $\text{Na}_2\text{SiO}_3$.
walkthrough:
Combine base plus acid oxide**
Basic $\text{Na}_2\text{O}$ neutralises acidic $\text{SiO}_2$ directly with no water or gas involved. The atoms simply combine: $$\text{Na}_2\text{O} + \text{SiO}_2 \rightarrow \text{Na}_2\text{SiO}_3$$ Check: 2 Na, 1 Si, 3 O on each side.
Final answer: $\mathrm{Na_2O + SiO_2 \rightarrow Na_2SiO_3}$

hints: Recall the general pattern for thermal decomposition of a carbonate: carbonate breaks down on heating to the oxide plus carbon dioxide.
walkthrough:
Apply the carbonate rule**
Heating a carbonate drives off $\text{CO}_2$ and leaves the metal oxide behind. For sodium carbonate: $$\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 \rightarrow \text{Na}_2\text{O} + \text{CO}_2$$ The equation is already balanced with 2 Na, 1 C and 3 O on each side.
Final answer: $\mathrm{Na_2CO_3 \rightarrow Na_2O + CO_2}$
